lead: A starter must turn a cold engine fast enough for fuel and compression to produce the first firings. It must supply cranking torque against compression, friction and oil drag, and hold a minimum cranking speed while the battery sags under hundreds of amperes. Petrol engines need less cranking effort than diesels. The same requirement appears in every car, bus and generator set: choose a starter and battery that crank the engine at the coldest expected temperature. This chapter sets out torque, speed, power and the stable cranking point.
prereq: You need: battery design and battery ratings for cranking current, and the four-stroke engine cycle.

blocks.text: Cranking is rotating the engine before it fires. The starter applies torque T (N·m) at the flywheel ring gear. Engine speed N is in revolutions per minute (rpm). Angular speed ω is in radians per second:

blocks.where: N is engine speed in rpm; ω is angular speed in rad/s; 2π rad is one revolution and 60 s is one minute.

blocks.text: Cranking power P (W) is the rate of doing cranking work:

blocks.where: T is cranking torque in N·m; ω is angular speed in rad/s; P is cranking power in W.

blocks.text: Power needs both torque and speed. A starter that gives 65 N·m at stall produces no cranking power because ω = 0. At 200 rpm and 45 N·m, ω = 20.94 rad/s and P = 45 × 20.94 = 942 W.

Minimum starting speed is the lowest cranking speed for reliable first firing. Petrol engines typically need about 60–100 rpm; diesels need about 100–200 rpm. Below this, compression leaks past rings, mixture velocity is low and combustion may not sustain. Cranking torque must also exceed the peak compression torque of the next cylinder. A four-cylinder petrol engine may need 30–50 N·m; a diesel of similar size can need much more.

sections.h3: Engine resistance and the stable cranking point

blocks.text: Engine resistance torque comes from compression, ring and bearing friction, valve-train friction, and pumping air through throttles and ports. It rises with speed: faster cranking means more friction and more pumping work per second. Starter torque falls with speed, as a series DC motor does. Plot both against speed. Their intersection is the stable cranking point. Below it, starter torque is larger, so speed rises. Above it, resistance is larger, so speed falls. The engine settles at the intersection.

At 200 rpm the starter curve in the figure gives T = 65 − 0.1 × 200 = 45 N·m. The resistance curve gives 10 + 0.1 × 200 = 30 N·m, so the engine still accelerates. The curves meet when 65 − 0.1N = 10 + 0.1N, giving N = 275 rpm and T = 37.5 N·m. Real curves are measured on a cold engine and change with temperature.

sections.h3: Design and temperature effects; battery sag

blocks.text: Compression ratio is the ratio of cylinder volume at bottom dead centre to volume at top dead centre. A diesel may use 16:1 to 22:1; a petrol engine may use 8:1 to 12:1. Higher compression raises peak pressure and cranking torque. Larger displacement and more cylinders raise total torque. Cold oil has higher viscosity, so friction rises and cranking speed falls. A cold battery also has higher internal resistance and less available capacity. A diesel therefore needs a larger battery and a stronger starter for the same swept volume.
Battery terminal voltage under cranking is:

blocks.where: V is terminal voltage in V; E is open-circuit emf in V; I is cranking current in A; R<sub>int</sub> is battery internal resistance in Ω.

blocks.text: A starter may draw several hundred amperes. Even 0.01 Ω gives a 3 V drop at 300 A. Lower terminal voltage reduces starter torque, which reduces speed, which raises current and deepens the sag. This is why poor terminals or a flat battery prevent cranking.

figure.caption: Starter torque falls with speed and engine resistance rises; the lines meet at 275 rpm and 37.5 N·m, and at 200 rpm the starter gives 45 N·m.

spec.aria: Starter torque falls from 65 N·m at 0 rpm to 35 N·m at 300 rpm while engine resistance rises from 10 to 40 N·m; at 200 rpm the starter torque is 45 N·m.

examples.question: A four-cylinder petrol engine needs 45 N·m of cranking torque at 200 rpm. Calculate the cranking power and the angular speed.
steps: Find power: P = Tω = 45 N·m × 20.94 rad/s = 942.5 W, taken as 942 W.
examples.answer: The cranking power is 942 W, or about 0.942 kW, at an angular speed of 20.94 rad/s.
examples.check:
import math
T = 45
N = 200
omega = 2 * math.pi * N / 60
P = T * omega
print(round(omega, 2))
print(round(P, 0))
print(round(P / 1000, 3))

traps: High torque at zero speed is not cranking power: P = Tω = 0 at stall.
Do not use engine rpm directly in P = Tω; convert to rad/s first. Using 200 instead of 20.94 gives a power about 9.55 times too large.
Diesel cranking torque is higher mainly because of high compression ratio, not because diesel fuel has higher calorific value during cranking.
Battery voltage sag under cranking current is not the same as battery capacity in Ah; a battery can have enough Ah and still fail cold cranking.
The stable cranking point is the intersection of starter torque and engine resistance curves, not the starter's maximum torque.

quiz.q: Define cranking torque and cranking speed.
quiz.a: Cranking torque is the torque applied by the starter to rotate the engine before firing, in N·m. Cranking speed is the engine speed during cranking, usually in rpm.

quiz.q: Why does engine resistance torque rise with cranking speed?
quiz.a: Friction and pumping work per second increase as speed rises, so resistance torque from rings, bearings, valve train and gas pumping becomes larger.

quiz.q: An engine needs 60 N·m of cranking torque at 150 rpm. Find the cranking power.
A petrol engine cranks at 120 rpm in warm weather but only 60 rpm cold. Using the stable cranking point idea, explain why cold cranking may fail.
quiz.a: Cold oil raises engine resistance and the cold battery sags more, so the starter torque curve falls. The intersection moves to a lower speed. If it falls below the minimum starting speed, first firing is unreliable.

quiz.q: State typical minimum cranking speed ranges for petrol and diesel engines.
quiz.a: Petrol engines typically need about 60–100 rpm; diesel engines typically need about 100–200 rpm.

quiz.q: Why does battery terminal voltage fall during cranking?
quiz.a: The starter draws a very large current. The battery internal resistance causes a voltage drop I × R<sub>int</sub>, so terminal voltage V = E − IR<sub>int</sub> is lower than the open-circuit emf E.

quiz.q: A 12 V battery has open-circuit emf 12.6 V and internal resistance 0.015 Ω. The starter draws 300 A. Find the terminal voltage.
quiz.a: Voltage drop = I × R<sub>int</sub> = 300 × 0.015 = 4.5 V. Terminal voltage V = 12.6 − 4.5 = 8.1 V.

quiz.q: Why is a starter with very high stall torque but low speed not always better for cranking?
quiz.a: Cranking power is P = Tω, so speed matters. A high stall torque at zero speed gives zero power. The starter must reach the engine's minimum starting speed at the stable cranking point.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cars increasingly use integrated starter-generators and 48 V mild-hybrid systems, where one machine cranks the engine and recovers braking energy. Cold-cranking simulation combines battery models, oil viscosity models and engine friction maps. Search for 'cold cranking simulator', 'starter torque-speed curve' and '48 V integrated starter generator'.
